title: On-load measurement method for the reliability of distribution transformers
author: Adesina, Abdulkareem, et al.

steps.title: Pre‑inspect selected substation
steps.instruction: Visit the chosen overloaded or troublesome distribution‑transformer substation and verify the source of supply, condition of high‑tension and low‑tension lines, overall neatness, proper connections of cables, lugs, bushings, earthing, feeder pillar, and confirm availability of the 33 kV or 11 kV feeder that feeds the transformer.

steps.title: Confirm fault‑free energized network
steps.instruction: Ensure the DT substation is on line, fault‑free, and receiving electricity supply.

steps.title: Connect Fluke 435 to transformer
steps.instruction: Attach one section of the Fluke 435 Power Quality and Energy Analyzer (PQEA) to the low‑voltage bushings at the secondary terminals of the on‑line DT.

steps.title: Connect Fluke 435 to feeder
steps.instruction: Attach the other section of the Fluke 435 to the incomer cable terminals at the feeder‑pillar side of the substation.

steps.title: Calibrate measurement duration and interval
steps.instruction: Calibrate the Fluke 435: set the experiment duration time (T) and the recording interval (t). For case study 1 (500 kVA) use T = 50 min for voltage, current and frequency measurements and T = 60 min for apparent power, reactive power and power‑factor measurements, with t = 10 min; for case study 2 (300 kVA) use T = 60 min (1 hour) with t = 10 min.

steps.title: Ground transformer and analyzer
steps.instruction: Provide a proper grounding connection for both the distribution transformer and the Fluke 435 (POAE) machine.

steps.title: Set measurement parameters
steps.instruction: On the Fluke 435, program the following parameters to be logged: RMS voltage (single‑phase and three‑phase), RMS current, frequency, apparent power, reactive power, active power, and power factor.

steps.title: Take conventional clamp‑on readings
steps.instruction: Using a Fluke 355 clamp‑on ammeter, manually measure voltage and current on each low‑voltage cable between the DT secondary bushings and the feeder pillar for later comparison with the PQEA data.

steps.title: Power on the analyzer
steps.instruction: Switch ON the Fluke 435 (PQEA) after all connections are verified.

steps.title: Record data for set duration
steps.instruction: Allow the Fluke 435 to remain ON for the calibrated duration time (T) while it automatically records the selected parameters at each interval (t).

steps.title: Disconnect and transport equipment
steps.instruction: When the duration T elapses, disconnect the PQEA equipment and transport it to the laboratory/office for further processing.

steps.title: Download and analyze results
steps.instruction: Using a personal computer, download the recorded data from the PQEA at the 10‑minute interval, then create graphs of each parameter (voltage, current, frequency, powers, power factor) using Microsoft Excel.

description: On case study 1, the obtained phase to neutral voltage ranges from 167.98 V to 219.58 V while the phase to phase rms voltage ranges from 343.68 V to 393.82 V. The two categories of voltage fall within the acceptable limits of standards of 230 V and 415 V respectively. The load on this transformer is not balanced because the 3 phases are not having the same values or values that are relatively closed. The operational frequency was between 50.318 Hz to 50.446 Hz, hence the operation is considered stable. The peak active power, apparent power and reactive power are 130.12 kW at 10:21:11 am, 133.24 kVA at 10:21:11 am and 30.94 kVAr at 10:11:11 am respectively. In this case, the peak power (i.e. all categories of power) did not occur the same time as it can be seen in the DT substation 2 later. The percentage of reactive power to active power in this DT network is 22.59% which is relatively alright by standards considering the values of average AP and RP. Lines Power factor is excellently alright, and they are within the range of minimum value of 0.96 and maximum value of 0.99 across the three phases. The network power factor ranges from 0.96 to 0.99 and the overall average network power factor was estimated to be 0.97. Considering the average apparent power value of 126.94 kVA loading of this DT with its 500kVA rated capacity, implies the percentage loading of this DT as at that hour was 25.39%.
